questions.question: How was the grandfather? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** He was **thin and frail**. He was very weak and **his hands used to tremble**. His eyesight was poor and he walked slowly. He had lost almost all his teeth and hair.

**What the passage says.**

> "The old grandfather had become very thin frail. He was very weak and his hands trembled."

**Why the details matter.** The trembling hands are the whole cause of the story: they make him drop food and spill milk, and it is these small accidents — not any fault of the old man — that the young couple punish by banishing him to a corner with a wooden bowl.

questions.question: Why was it difficult for grandfather to eat and drink? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Grandfather was **weak**, and **his hands would shake**, so it made it difficult to eat. Roti, rice and curry fell from his fingers on to his clothes and the floor, and milk spilled over the table cloth.

**What the passage says.**

> "Grandfather's hand would shake and it made eating rather difficult. Roti, rice and curry fell from his fingers on his clothes and onto the floor."

**The couple's reaction.** Instead of helping him, the son and daughter-in-law "soon became irritated", disliked changing the dirty table cloth, and finally moved him to a mat on the floor with a wooden bowl. The story's point is that the fault lay in their impatience, not in his hands.

questions.question: Why did the daughter-in-law scold the grandfather? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Because when he ate, **food fell on his clothes and milk got spilled over the table cloth** — and once he even **broke some plates and glasses**. She was tired of cleaning up after him.

**Detail from the passage.** "He did not complain yet the young man and his wife scolded him for dropping food and spilling milk over the floor." The scolding is the injustice the story sets out to expose, and it is answered by the child's remark about the wooden bowl.

questions.question: Why did the young man sit speechless? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** On hearing his son's words — that the little boy was making **a wooden bowl for his father and mother to eat from when they grew old** — he sat speechless. He realised what he and his wife had done.

**Explanation.** The four-year-old's innocent reply, "You and Ma can eat your food from this bowl when you grow old like grandfather", struck the parents "and made them realize what they had done". Their own treatment of the old man was being handed back to them by a child who had simply observed and imitated them. That is why the young man had no words, and why tears started to fall down his wife's cheeks.

questions.question: What should the parents do for children? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The parents should **set a good example to their children**, because children always **observe and imitate** their mother and father. A wise parent realises this and tries to be a good role model, besides giving a happy home, food, clothes and education.

**The passage's own words.**

> "Children always observe and imitate their mother and father throughout their lives... It is also their duty as parents to set a good example."

**Application to the story.** The young man and his wife thought they were teaching their son nothing by putting the grandfather in a corner; in fact they were teaching him exactly how old people are to be treated, and he learned the lesson so well that he began making the bowl for them.

questions.question: Find the words from the passage which mean the same as: (i) chide (para-2) (ii) to copy (para-3).
questions.answer:
**Answer.** (i) chide — **scolded**; (ii) to copy — **imitate**.

**As used in the passage.**

> "The young man and his wife **scolded** him for dropping food and spilling milk over the floor."

> "Children always observe and **imitate** their mother and father throughout their lives."

**Note.** Write only the single word required; "chide" is a milder word than "scold", but the passage's own choice is the answer the examiner expects.

questions.question: On the basis of your reading of the passage on conserving wildlife, make notes on it. You may use headings, sub-headings and abbreviations; also give a suitable title.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Title: The Need for Preserving Wildlife**

1. **Reasons for conserving plants**
   1.1 essential for our survival
   1.2 capable of using solar energy to make food

2. **Role in energy production**
   2.1 first link in the food chain
   2.2 gives out oxygen as a by-product

3. **Need for wildlife**
   3.1 animals and plants live together in communities
   3.2 removal of one species alters the ecosystem

4. **Effect of destruction of wildlife**
   4.1 removal of rain forest reduces local rainfall
   4.2 big cause of pollution; fields may become deserts

5. **Uses of wildlife**
   5.1 supplies us food
   5.2 provides materials and chemicals of daily use

6. **Effects of exploitation**
   6.1 species cannot replenish themselves
   6.2 no longer available to us

7. **Our ignorance**
   7.1 we understand the biology of only a tiny fraction of wildlife
   7.2 we do not know what useful materials we lose

**Key to abbreviations.** eco-sys. – ecosystem; rainfor. – rain forest; sp. – species; agri. – agriculture; cons. – conservation.

questions.question: Write a summary of the wildlife-conservation passage in about 80 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** We need to conserve our wildlife. Plants use solar energy and are essential for our survival; they are the first link in the food chain and give out oxygen. Removal of the rain forest reduces rainfall, and the fields become deserts. Wildlife supplies us with food items, daily-used materials and medicines, but if we exploit these species to the point where they cannot replenish themselves, they will no longer be available. Without wildlife there is no life.

**Word count.** About 85 words. The summary follows the passage's order — plants, animals, destruction, uses, warning — which is what the marking scheme looks for.

questions.question: You are the Principal of a +2 school, Ranchi. Write a notice for the school notice board advising the students to stop chewing tobacco products.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**S. S. +2 HIGH SCHOOL, RANCHI**

**NOTICE**

*12 July 2017*

**STOP CHEWING TOBACCO PRODUCTS**

It has been noticed with concern that some students are chewing *gutkha*, *khaini* and other tobacco products inside the school premises and near the gate. These products are **injurious to health** and are **banned by law** near educational institutions.

All students are hereby advised to stop chewing tobacco products with immediate effect. Defaulters will be punished and their parents informed. The co-operation of every student is expected.

**Principal**
S. S. +2 High School, Ranchi

**Format points.** Name of the institution, the word NOTICE, the date, a short body in the third person giving the **instruction** and the **consequence**, and the signature with the designation — all within 50 words, boxed.

questions.question: You have an old car in good condition which you want to sell. Write an advertisement to be published in a newspaper.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**FOR SALE**

A **Maruti 800** in excellent working condition, **1998 model**. Owner leaving abroad. Giving an average of **16 km a litre**. All accessories intact. **Expected price below Rs. 1.1 lacs.** Interested persons may contact **Amarnath, 26, Saket Nagar, Ranchi-2. M. No.: 9211420143**.

**Format points.** A classified advertisement begins with a one-word heading in capitals, packs make, model, year, condition, mileage, price and contact into a single paragraph, and omits all forms of address or salutation. Every word is charged, so no sentence should be wasted.

questions.question: Your school celebrated Teacher's Day on 5th September. Prepare a report to be sent to a local daily newspaper.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**TEACHER'S DAY CELEBRATION**

*Staff Reporter*

**Ranchi, 5 September 2017.** On 5th September, the birth anniversary of the former Vice-President **Dr. S. Radhakrishnan**, Teacher's Day has been celebrated in our school campus.

In this programme the **Education Minister of Jharkhand** and the **Director of the school** were chief guest and special guest. On this occasion different types of cultural programme were presented. Our chief guest was introduced to the students, and he spoke about the contribution of Dr. S. Radhakrishnan and the place of the teacher in society. In this programme winners among the students were awarded by the chief guest and the Director of our school. A welcome speech was delivered by the Principal and, at the last movement of the programme, the achievement and future plans of our school were expressed by the Director.

The programme ended with a vote of thanks and the National Anthem. The whole campus was decorated with rangoli and paper flowers made by the students themselves.

**Mohit**
Dated: June 10th, ABC School

**Format points.** A report carries a headline, the reporter's name, the date and place, the events in sequence in the past tense, and the names of the guests and the prizes.

questions.question: Write a report on a fire accident that you have witnessed.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**THE FIRE ACCIDENT — A REPORT**

*By Praveen, Reporter, The Times of India*

**Shahdara, 15 April.** A devastating fire broke out last night in the **Central Market**. The fire was noticed at about 10 p.m., and in no time it engulfed the whole market. This reporter happened to pass that way and at once rang up the fire brigade.

The fire brigade did arrive very soon, but it took some time to locate the water hydrant, which was quite a number of feet away. In the meantime the fire had become very dangerous. A large number of people gathered there, and each tried in his own way to put out the fire. They threw buckets of water on the rising flames, but it was not of much use. At last the fire brigade set to work, and after continuous spraying of water for about two hours the fire was brought under control. Many shops were completely destroyed and the damage is estimated to be more than **ten crores**.

The cause of the fire is believed to be a **short circuit**. Luckily there was no loss of life.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, place and date, what happened, when and where, the rescue effort, the loss and the probable cause — the last two are what make a report informative rather than merely exciting.

questions.question: You are disturbed by loud music played at night. Write a letter to the Editor of *The Times of India* expressing your feelings in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**27, Harmu Housing Colony**
**Ranchi**
**18 August 2017**

The Editor
*The Times of India*
Ranchi

**Subject: Nuisance caused by loud music played at night**

Sir

Through the columns of your esteemed daily I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to the nuisance of loud music played late at night in our locality.

For the last several weeks, marriage processions and open-air parties in the community hall near my house play film songs at full volume until two or three in the morning. The Supreme Court has already fixed a limit on the sound level, but the rules are flouted openly. Old people cannot sleep, students preparing for examinations are distracted, and small children wake up crying. Repeated complaints to the organisers and to the police have produced no result.

I request the district administration to enforce the noise-pollution rules strictly and to fine offenders.

Yours faithfully
**Anand Kumar**

**Format points.** The problem, its effect on specific groups, the legal position and a workable remedy; a letter to the editor must remain restrained.

questions.question: You are the Head boy of St. Paul's College, Ranchi. Write an application to the Principal asking for permission to organise a class picnic, in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**The Principal**
St. Paul's College
Ranchi
20 May 2016

**Subject: Permission to organise a class picnic**

Sir

I am a student of XII A and also the prefect of the class. All the students of our class are now wanting a picnic, as the season is asking at present. As a prefect of the class, I am asking permission from you to organise a class picnic so that the students can be refreshed.

We propose to go to **Patratu Dam** on Saturday, the 27th of May, by a hired bus leaving at 7 a.m. and returning by 6 p.m. Twenty-eight students and two teachers will go, and the entire cost will be borne by the students themselves. A teacher will accompany us and a first-aid box will be carried.

We will be grateful to you for your kind permission.

Yours faithfully
**John**

**Format points.** Address and date, addressee, subject line, the proposal with **date, place, time, number of students and arrangement for safety**, and a formal close — within 125 words.

questions.question: Write an article on the performance of the Indian team in the Olympic Games, 2016, in about 150–200 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**INDIA AT RIO: A RECORD OF HONEST STRUGGLE**

The 2016 Olympic Games at Rio de Janeiro will be remembered in India with mixed feelings. Our contingent of over a hundred athletes came home with just **two medals** — a silver won by **P. V. Sindhu** in badminton and a bronze by **Sakshi Malik** in wrestling — and no gold. On the medal table India stood far below countries with a fraction of its population.

Yet the Games were not a failure. Sakshi Malik's bronze was India's first medal in women's wrestling, and she won it after being two points down in a bout she seemed to have lost. Sindhu's run to the final included a victory over the world number one and brought badminton into drawing rooms that had never watched it. Dipa Karmakar finished fourth in the vault, missing a medal by a hair, and the hockey team reached the quarter-finals after years of decline.

The lessons are plain. India needs better **sports infrastructure**, professional coaching at the school level and honest selection. Cricket's monopoly of money and attention must be shared. Rio showed the talent is there; what is missing is the system that turns talent into medals.

**Format points.** An article on a current issue balances achievement and criticism, gives facts and figures, and ends with a suggestion rather than a complaint.

questions.question: Write an article on 'Price Hike' in about 150–200 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**PRICE HIKE IN THE PRICES OF ESSENTIAL COMMODITIES**

Price hike has become a day-to-day affair in India. One is not sure about the price of an item the next day. Thus living has become a costly affair. Lower income group people are the worst sufferers. The price graph of essential items of a common man's consumption, e.g. rice, pulse, and wheat, has been rising higher and higher. Dream of a free and prosperous India has been shattered. It is surprising that the prices of computers, cars, colour TVs etc. have drastically fallen, but the prices of tea, salt, rice, gas and pulses are at an abnormal height.

Who is responsible for price hike — the government, the traders or the producers? It is a paradox in India that the farmer who feeds the nation sleeps hungry at night. The poor farmer is compelled to sell his product at half the price of the market. It is the middlemen and hoarders who actually control the flow of commodities in the market. They create artificial scarcity in the market and sell them at a higher rate. Since these traders extend monetary help to the politicians in elections, the latter cannot take drastic action against them. Government officials also take advantage of the situation. Thus there is no effective mechanism to check it.

No nation can claim to have prospered when millions of its people are deprived of their basic needs. This is high time that the administration must take drastic action against these black marketeers and profiteers so that the fruit of democracy reaches the last man in the ladder.

**Format points.** Title, figures or examples, causes, remedies and a conclusion — the article above moves from effect to responsibility to appeal.

questions.question: Name the poet and the poem of the extract: 'Fisherman in cold sea / Would not harm whales / and the man gathering salt / would look at his hurt hands.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **Keeping Quiet**; poet — **Pablo Neruda**.

**Context.** In these lines the poet imagines what the silence of a "count to twelve" would do to ordinary labour. The fisherman on the cold sea would stop harming the whales, and the salt-gatherer would look at his own hurt hands. The stillness would not stop work for ever; it would make each worker see what his work costs.

questions.question: What should the fishermen not do? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Fishermen **would not harm the whales**. In the quietness of the moment they would stop hunting and hurting the creatures of the sea.

**Explanation.** Neruda sets this beside the salt-gatherer's hurt hands and the men preparing for war: all of them would pause, look at what they are doing and spare something — the whale, the body, the enemy. The poem does not say that fishing ends, only that in a moment of silence a fisherman sees the whale as something other than a catch.

questions.question: Why do fishermen go to the sea? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Fishermen go to the sea to **catch fish and earn their livelihood**. The sea is their place of work, where they hunt and bring home their catch for the market and for food.

**Explained in context.** In "Keeping Quiet" the fisherman is shown "in the cold sea", doing the hard, dangerous work by which he lives. The poem's point is not that this work is evil but that it is done without reflection: in the planned silence he would pause long enough to notice "the whales" he kills. The contrast between his need to earn and the harm he does is exactly the "sadness of never understanding ourselves" that the poet wants to end.

questions.question: Name the poet of the extract: 'Aunt Jennifer's fingers fluttering through wool / Find even the ivory needle hard to pull. / The massive weight of Uncle's wedding band / Sits heavily upon Aunt Jennifer's hand.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poet — **Adrienne Rich**; poem — **Aunt Jennifer's Tigers**.

**Context.** These lines close the poem. The aunt's fingers flutter nervously through the wool, and even the ivory needle is hard for her to pull; the "massive weight of Uncle's wedding band" sits heavily on her hand. The ring is the poem's central symbol: it stands for a marriage that has weighed the woman down and left her "terrified" and mastered.

questions.question: What is Aunt Jennifer doing? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Aunt Jennifer is **embroidering tigers on a panel of cloth**. Her fingers move fluttering through the wool, and she finds even the ivory needle hard to pull because of the weight of her wedding band.

**Explanation.** The tigers she creates "prance across the screen", "bright topaz denizens of a world of green", fearless of the men beneath the tree. In making them she gives shape to the boldness she cannot show in her own life, and the poem contrasts the quick, certain tigers with the trembling hands that stitch them.

questions.question: Why is Aunt Jennifer upset? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Aunt Jennifer is upset because of her **unhappy, oppressive marriage**. The "massive weight of Uncle's wedding band" sits heavily on her hand, and she lives "terrified" under a husband's will, with no freedom of her own.

**Explanation.** Adrienne Rich shows an ordinary housewife who can express courage only through her needle. Her fingers flutter and even the needle is hard to pull, yet the tigers she embroiders are bold and unafraid. The poem's sadness is that the woman and her creation will never meet: the tigers go on prancing, but "Aunt Jennifer's tigers will go on prancing" while her hands lie still — the freedom is only in the cloth.

questions.question: What were the things on the wall of the classroom? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The walls of the slum classroom were decorated with the pictures of **'Shakespeare', 'buildings with domes', 'world maps' and 'beautiful valleys'** — "a sun", "a lover and his lass" and "civilised domes".

**Explanation.** In Stephen Spender's "An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum" these are the "donations" of a school inspector or a benefactor — a map, a portrait, a scenic calendar. The poem's charge is that such pictures are a mockery: a map which promises "the world" to children whose entire world is "the slag heap". The chapter is now outside the current syllabus but the question remains in older sets.

questions.question: What according to Pablo Neruda would be an exotic moment? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Uncalled-for and unjustified rush and hurry has made our lives miserable and difficult. The poet advises that we should stop rushing and hurrying, and that the noise of engines and machines should stop for once; **that moment would be an exotic, unusual and exciting moment**.

**Explanation.** In "Keeping Quiet" he asks us to count to twelve and "keep still", without speaking "in any language" and without moving our arms so much. He calls that stillness "an exotic moment" — strange, unfamiliar, almost foreign to our noisy lives — in which "we would all be together in a sudden strangeness". He is careful to add that he does not want total inactivity or death: "What I want should not be confused with total inactivity.

questions.question: How is a thing of beauty a joy for ever? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** According to John Keats, to experience a beautiful thing is **a joy for ever**. The loveliness of the thing of beauty is **ever increasing** and its effect on man is eternal. It **never fades**, it never turns into nothingness. It gives us peace of mind and a sleep full of pleasant dreams, and removes the pall of sadness that clouds and darkens our spirit.

**Explanation.** Keats's examples are the sun, the moon, the old and young trees, the daffodils, the clear rills, the mid-forest brake and the musk-rose blooms. Each of them, he says, makes a "bower quiet for us" and pours "some shape of beauty" into the dark "spirits" of the world — which is why beauty is more than a passing pleasure.

questions.question: What was on sale at the roadside stand? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** There were the **ordinary things of daily use for sale** — "wild berries" and "crook-necked gourd" — **sold in wooden quarts**, and the stand also offered "crook-necked grounds with silvery hard lumps".

**Explanation.** In Robert Frost's "A Roadside Stand" the hut sells the produce of a poor farm: berries, squash and gourds, set out in the hope that "the city money" will stop for them. The poet's bitter observation is that the polished cars "halt" only to ask the way, and the villagers' produce rots unsold beside a stand built out of "the back of the house" and old tin.

questions.question: Who was M. Hamel? Why was he sad? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** M. Hamel was a **school teacher of French** in Alsace who had taught in the same school for **forty years**. He was sad because he had to leave the school and the district after the German order that only German would be taught.

**Explanation.** In "The Last Lesson" Franz finds the teacher in his Sunday clothes, and hears him say from his chair that this is the last French lesson. M. Hamel's sadness is not only personal: he feels the humiliation of a people forbidden their own language, and he blames himself and the parents for not having insisted on learning it while they could.

questions.question: Which language would replace French in schools? Why? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **German** would replace French in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine, because an order had come **from Berlin** after the Prussian victory in the war — "it was the order from Berlin" that "only German will be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine".

**Explanation.** The language is imposed by the conqueror as an instrument of rule: if a people loses its language, M. Hamel says, it is as if they held "the key to their prison". That is why the old villagers come to the class and why the last lesson turns into a lesson in patriotism.

questions.question: Who was Mukesh? What was his ambition? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Young Mukesh belongs to a **family of bangle-makers in Firozabad**. He doesn't like the profession of bangle-making. He **entertains new dreams**: he wants to be **his own master**, he wants to become a **motor mechanic** and will go to a garage and learn his art.

**Explanation.** In "Lost Spring" Mukesh's family has worked in the glass furnaces for generations, and his grandmother has never seen a full meal in her life. Mukesh, however, says "I will be a motor mechanic" and even speaks of driving a car, which Anees Jung calls a "dream" in a town where the boys' eyes are "dusted with the mirage of the bangle trade". His ambition is modest and yet, in that setting, almost heroic.

questions.question: What is the meaning of Saheb-e-Alam? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Saheb's name is **"Saheb-e-Alam"**. It means **"lord of the universe"**. It is quite ironic that "Saheb-e-Alam" is a young barefoot ragpicker who scrounges for gold in the garbage dumps of Delhi.

**Explanation.** In "Lost Spring" Anees Jung points out the gap between the grand name and the life: the boy who is called the lord of the universe owns nothing, has no shoes and hunts for a coin in other people's rubbish. The irony is the author's way of showing the "lost spring" of Indian childhood — a season of life that is never allowed to arrive.

questions.question: Who was Danny Casey? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Danny Casey was a young **footballer** — a player of the Irish club **Manchester United**, who had come to England from Dublin. He was **Sophie's hero** and the centre of her fantasies.

**Explanation.** In A. R. Barton's "Going Places" Sophie invents a meeting with Danny Casey by the canal and tells her brother Geoff that the player promised to come again next Saturday. She waits for him, and he does not come — which is the point of the story: the dream is more comfortable than the reality, and Sophie prefers to keep it.

questions.question: How did the crofter earn thirty kronor? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The crofter's **cow (bossy) was extraordinary**. She gave milk for the creamery every day. Last month he had received **thirty kronor in payment**.

**Explanation.** In Selma Lagerlöf's "The Rattrap" the old man proudly shows the peddler the three ten-kronor notes the creamery paid him and hides them in a leather pouch. The peddler steals them the next morning and is thereafter a hunted man — until Edla's kindness at the Ramsjö ironworks makes him return them.

questions.question: Draw a character sketch of Franz. (Answer in about 100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Little Franz was a student of a school in Alsace. M. Hamel was his school master. Franz was **not a brilliant student**. He didn't prepare his lesson on participles. When he was asked to recite, he got mixed up and confused. He was **not particularly interested in going to school**. Nor did he show any interest in M. Hamel's teaching. He was greatly scared of Hamel's scolding; he was always in dread of "the great ruler that M. Hamel kept under his arm". He knew how "cranky" M. Hamel was.

However, Franz had to change his opinion about M. Hamel. An order had come from Berlin that German language would be taught in the schools of French districts of Alsace and Lorraine. When he came to know that it was the last lesson that M. Hamel was going to deliver, his views about him changed. He began to respect the man who had spent 40 years in the same school. He felt sorry that he had neglected learning French. He shared M. Hamel's views about French: it was the most beautiful language in the world. It was a great pity that from the next day M. Hamel would not teach them French — he would leave them for good. A new master would come to teach German. He sarcastically remarked, "Will they make them sing in German, even the pigeons?"

M. Hamel actually began to like and respect him. He liked how M. Hamel came in his best clothes in honour of his last lesson. His views about the French took a patriotic turn. He listened to M. Hamel's last lesson with rapt attention and respect.

**Character in a word.** Franz is the ordinary, careless schoolboy whose eyes are opened only when the thing he has neglected is taken away — the story's device for making the reader feel the loss.

questions.question: Describe life in Seemapuri. (Answer in about 100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Seemapuri is a place on the periphery of Delhi — the national capital of India. It is a settlement of more than **10,000 ragpickers**. These people came from **Bangladesh in 1971**. For most of these people ragpicking is the only means of their livelihood. They live there without an identity and without permits. They do have ration cards that enable them to vote and buy grain. **Food is more important for them than their identity.**

Children grow up to become partners in survival. An army of barefoot children appears in the morning with their plastic bags on their shoulders. They disappear by noon. Garbage has a different meaning for children. For them it is wrapped in 'wonder'. They may find a rupee, even a ten rupee note or a silver coin. There is always hope of finding more.

Seemapuri may be on the periphery of Delhi, yet it is miles away from it, metaphorically. Ragpickers live in structures of mud. They have roofs of tin and tarpaulin. There is no sewage, drainage or running water. It is unimaginable that it is a part of Delhi, the capital of India. Delhi represents the developed and prosperous face of India, but Seemapuri is a little hell.

**What the contrast means.** The chapter's argument is that the "developed" and the "lost" India exist side by side, and that the distance between them is not measured in miles but in opportunity.

questions.question: Draw a character sketch of the Tiger King. (Answer in about 100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The Maharaja of Pratibandapuram, **Sir Jilani Jung Jung Bahadur**, had so many titles and sub-names that it was often shortened to the **Tiger King**. The royal infant was born in the hour of the Bull. He would have to meet his death one day; this is what the chief astrologer predicted. The Bull and the Tiger are enemies, and so his death would "come from the Tiger".

Crown prince Jung Jung Bahadur grew taller and stronger day by day. The boy drank the milk of an English cow, was brought up by an English governess, was tutored in English by an Englishman — he saw nothing but English films. The state had been with the Court of Wards, and when he grew to twenty he took the reign in his hands.

The Maharaja was a man of determination. He continued his campaign of tiger-hunting with rare single-mindedness: within a span of ten years he killed 70 tigers. When tigers became extinct in his kingdom, he hit upon a plan. His master strategy was to marry a girl of a state with a large tiger population, and he killed five or six tigers on each visit to his father-in-law's state — 99 in all.

The Tiger King was a man of self-respect; he could pay any price to maintain it. He refused permission to a high-ranking British officer to hunt tigers in his state, and had to give a bribe worth three lakh rupees to retain his kingdom. He knew how to take work from his ministers: he used the dewan to find a suitable girl for his marriage and doubled the tax on those exempted earlier. He was hot-headed and threatened to dismiss the dewan.

**The irony.** "It is ironical that the King who killed 99 tigers met his death by a wooden tiger." The hundredth tiger, a cheap wooden toy bought for his son's third birthday, took revenge upon him when a sliver from it pricked his hand and caused blood-poisoning.

questions.question: Why and how did Dr. Sadao help the prisoner of war to escape? Do you find him guilty of harbouring an enemy? (Answer in about 100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Dr. Sadao had given a **new lease of life to the American prisoner of war**. He and his wife Hana took a lot of pains to save his life. He did not want to throw him into the jaws of death again. He asked the young soldier to take his **private boat at night**. He should row in the cover of darkness to a **little island nearby**. The island was deserted, as nobody lived on it. The young American could live there until he saw a **Korean fishing boat pass by**. Many of them passed near the island. He put **food, bottled water and two quilts** in the boat. If the food ran out before he caught a boat, he could signal **two flashes**; he was not to signal in darkness because he could be seen. The young American came down into the darkness of the garden and escaped. The prisoner had gone **quite safe**.

**Guilt?** No, Dr. Sadao cannot be found guilty of harbouring an enemy. No doubt the nations of countries at war are considered enemies, but we should not forget that Sadao was a **doctor**, and for a doctor saving a dying man is the foremost priority. It doesn't matter if the dying man is an enemy.

questions.question: What does the chief astrologer tell to be the causes of the Maharaja's death? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The royal infant tells him that "all those who are born will one day have to die" — there is nothing new in it, and he wants to know the real cause of his death. The astrologer tells him that he is born in the **hour of the Bull**, and the Bull and the Tiger are enemies, therefore his death will "come from the **Tiger**".

**Explanation.** In Kalki's story this single prediction sets the whole plot in motion: the Maharaja devotes his life to killing tigers so that the prophecy cannot come true, and the hundredth tiger — a wooden toy — fulfils it exactly.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: When were India and Antarctica part of the same landmass? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** About **six hundred and fifty million years ago** a giant "amalgamated" southern supercontinent existed. It was called **Gondwana**. There was a time when India and Antarctica were part of the same landmass. It centred roughly around present-day Antarctica.

**Explanation.** In Tishani Doshi's "Journey to the End of the Earth", Gondwana had a much warmer climate and a huge variety of flora and fauna, and humans had not appeared. It broke apart about 500 million years later, and that break-up explains the present position of the continents and the climate patterns that Antarctica's ice now records.

questions.question: Who was Hana and where did Sadao meet her? How were they married? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Sadao and Hana first met each other **at an American professor's house**. But he had waited to fall in love with her until he was sure she was Japanese. His father would not have accepted her in the family unless she had been "pure" in her race.

**Explanation.** In "The Enemy" Hana is a Japanese girl who had lived long in America; she and Sadao met there while he was studying surgery. Their marriage was arranged after his return to Japan, and Hana becomes the one person in the house who shares the burden of the wounded American — she washes him, feeds him and keeps the servants from discovering the truth.

questions.question: What is wrong with Derry's face? How do people react when they look at it? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **One side of Derry's face was totally burnt.** People remind Derry that these are people even worse than him — he might be blind, dumb or maimed by birth. Sometimes people can be very cruel: a woman says, "Look at that... that's terrible you see."

**Explanation.** In Susan Hill's "On the Face of It" Derry's cheek was burnt by acid when he was a child, and he has withdrawn from people because of their stares and whispers. It is Mr. Lamb, with his tin leg and his "it's all relative" philosophy, who makes him see that other people's cruelty is their problem, not his.

questions.question: Describe Jack's style of storytelling. (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Storytelling had become a daily practice for Jack. Jack told his daughter a story out of his head in the evenings and for Saturday naps. This custom, begun when she was two, was itself now nearly two years old. All stories were the creation of Jack's mind, and he told them to his daughter, who listened to them with keen interest.

**Explanation.** In "Should Wizard Hit Mommy?" (a chapter now outside the current syllabus) Jack's formula never varies: a small creature named Roger — fish, squirrel or skunk — goes to the wise owl, is sent to the wizard, and has his problem changed. Jo, now four, has begun asking whether the wizard was right to change Roger, and her questions slowly break the comfortable ritual apart.
